name: Self-persuasion
statement: Arguments people produce themselves are said to change their own attitudes and behaviour more than the same arguments handed to them.
meaning: The claim is about who produced the argument, not about what the argument says. Someone asked why a rule matters writes the case for it, and the case is then their own. Lemmen and colleagues state the premise as the motivation to act coming from within the person, citing Aronson. Cognitive dissonance, which has its own entry here, is one proposed reason the procedure works rather than the procedure itself. Effort justification, also with an entry, revalues what effort bought, while this revalues a position the person argued. So the testable part is a comparison, and a study of it needs a condition in which somebody else supplies the arguments.

origin.who: Irving L. Janis and Bert T. King
origin.where: The Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology
origin.note: The paper is titled "The influence of role playing on opinion change" and ran at 49(2), 211-218. Its text is closed at the publisher and no repository copy is indexed by Unpaywall, OpenAlex or Semantic Scholar, so nothing about its design or its results is reported on this page. The name self-persuasion belongs to Elliot Aronson's 1999 article in American Psychologist, 54(11), 875-884, which is also closed.

evidence: Lemmen, Keizer, Bouman and Steg ran the comparison at Apenheul, a Dutch primate park. Signs at the entrance to the free-ranging enclosure either carried three arguments for not luring the squirrel monkeys, or asked visitors why they should not lure them, or carried both, or said nothing. Three observers dressed as visitors watched a marked area of 4 by 15 metres and recorded who broke the rule. Of 2,264 visitors, 17% lured the monkeys in the control condition, 7% where the arguments were given, z = 4.82, p < .001, and 7% where the question was asked, z = 4.82, p < .001. The two interventions did not differ, z = 0.09, p = .928, across the 1,013 visitors who saw one of them. Visitors given both signs broke the rule more often, at 11%, than visitors given the question alone, z = 2.12, p < .05. A questionnaire at the exit reached 350 visitors. Asking the question raised how important the rule was rated, from 5.73 to 6.03 on a seven-point scale, F(1, 345) = 6.48, p < .05, partial eta squared 0.018. Providing arguments did not, F(1, 345) = 0.69, p = .408. Damen, Müller, van Baaren and Dijksterhuis gave 120 Dutch students either arguments for a clean local environment or the task of writing those arguments themselves. Neither the persuasion type nor a preceding manipulation of felt agency moved attitudes on its own, both F values below 1. The two interacted, F(1, 116) = 9.20, p = .003, partial eta squared 0.07, and generating the arguments beat receiving them only among students who had just been made to feel in control, F(1, 116) = 7.35, p = .008.

replication.headline: Meta-analysis finds that advocating a behaviour, on its own, does not reliably beat doing nothing, while preregistered laboratory studies find an advantage over supplied arguments when generating them feels easy.
replication.detail: Priolo and colleagues meta-analysed 29 published and nine unpublished studies of induced hypocrisy, the two-step procedure in which people first advocate a desirable behaviour and then recall their own failures to follow it. The full procedure beat a control on intention, r = .35, 95% CI [.22, .46], across 19 studies, and on behaviour, r = .30, 95% CI [.10, .48], across ten. The advocacy step on its own did not beat a control on intention, r = .16, 95% CI [-.06, .36], across eight studies, and the full procedure beat advocacy alone, r = .30, 95% CI [.21, .37], across 16. Recalling transgressions without advocating anything did beat a control, r = .25, 95% CI [.08, .41], and adding advocacy to it changed nothing detectable, r = .18, 95% CI [-.04, .35], both across eight studies. Whether the procedure produced the discomfort the theory needs was inconclusive, r = .18, 95% CI [-.02, .36], across seven studies. Loman and colleagues showed 149 students an anti-alcohol poster framed either as an open question or as a statement, then measured how much beer they drank in a taste test. Condition made no difference, F(4, 140) = 0.76, p = .55, with a Bayes factor of 14.31 favouring the null over the model with condition in it. Xu and Wegener report five studies, two of them preregistered at 528 and 496 participants. Their abstract states that self-generated arguments beat other-generated arguments when people found generation easy, and that the advantage shrank when they found it hard. Catapano, Tormala and Rucker ran three preregistered experiments with 2,734 participants; their abstract reports that taking the perspective of someone holding the opposing view reduced attitude change after a counter-attitudinal argument-generation task.

study.cite: Priolo, D., Pelt, A., St. Bauzel, R., Rubens, L., Voisin, D., & Fointiat, V. (2019). Three decades of research on induced hypocrisy: A meta-analysis. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 45(12), 1681-1701.

limits: The structured figure on this page is Priolo and colleagues' estimate for advocacy alone against a control, pooled over eight induced-hypocrisy studies. It is not a replication of any single experiment, it belongs to one procedure rather than to the family, and there is no matching original figure to set beside it. Janis and King's 1954 paper and Aronson's 1999 article were not read for this entry, because both are closed and neither has an open copy indexed at Unpaywall, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar or Europe PMC. King and Janis's 1956 follow-up in Human Relations and Greenwald and Albert's 1968 paper in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology are named here for the same reason and were likewise not read. Xu and Wegener and Catapano and colleagues were read in abstract only, at Crossref. No preregistered direct replication of Janis and King was located in a search covering Crossref, PubMed, Europe PMC, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, Unpaywall and web search. Lemmen and colleagues assigned conditions to mornings rather than to individual visitors, and the observers watched unobtrusively while dressed as visitors. Their questionnaire condition means come from 350 people, a seventh of the number observed. Loman and colleagues used a forced taste test and raise the loss of free choice as a reason their posters may have done nothing. Damen and colleagues' 120 students are split four ways, so each cell holds about 30.
misreadings: The first misreading is that self-persuasion is a mechanism. It names a procedure, and dissonance is one candidate explanation of why the procedure might work. The second is that the advocacy step is what does the work. In the hypocrisy literature that step alone did not beat a control, while recalling one's own failures did, and Priolo and colleagues recommend keeping both steps to make the standard salient rather than because advocacy carries the effect. The third is that beating a do-nothing control demonstrates anything about self-persuasion. Lemmen and colleagues' question sign cut rule-breaking from 17% to 7%, and so did the sign that simply gave the reasons, by the same amount. The fourth is that more is better. Visitors who got the arguments and then the question broke the rule more often than visitors who got either alone. The phrase "saying is believing" also titles Higgins and Rholes's 1978 paper in the Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, which is about tuning a description to an audience and then remembering it that way, and is a different claim.
